Working with MICS sibling history data

Dennis M. Feehan with collaboration of Claude (Opus 5)

2026-08-22

mics-data.Rmd

UNICEF’s Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) collect sibling survival histories in some rounds, using a module closely related to the one in the DHS. prep_mics_sib_histories() prepares those data for the estimators in this package.

This vignette covers what MICS data looks like, how it differs from the DHS, and what we learned validating the package against published MICS estimates.

Which MICS surveys can be used

MICS has fielded two structurally different mortality modules under the same “MM” label, and only one of them is a sibling survival history.

MICS2 / MICS3 MICS4 / MICS5 MICS6 / MICS7
Method Indirect sisterhood Direct sibling history Direct sibling history
Usable here? No Yes Yes
Respondents All adults 15+ Women 15–49 Women 15–49
Brothers enumerated? No Yes Yes
Roster numbering — MM5–MM13 MM15–MM27
Estimand — Pregnancy-related Maternal and pregnancy-related

MICS2 and MICS3 collect summary sisterhood counts in the household questionnaire – no per-sibling roster, no ages at death – so they cannot be used with this package at all.

The direct sibling module is optional, and most surveys did not field it. The practical test is whether the survey ships an mm.sav file. Of 229 MICS surveys we examined, only 13 have a usable sibling history: 2 in MICS4, 7 in MICS5 and 4 in MICS6.

Two traps when building your own inventory:

  • MICS3’s mm.sav is the men’s file, not maternal mortality. It contains variables like MM4 “Man’s Line number” and mmweight “men’s sample weight”. Globbing for mm.sav will pick these up.
  • Surveys that did not field the module do not hide the roster in wm.sav – there simply are no MM variables.

You can check a survey before downloading it: the World Bank microdata catalog publishes full variable dictionaries without registration.

A minimal example

MICS publishes the roster as one row per reported sibling, so no reshaping is needed.

library(siblingsurvival)
library(haven)

mm <- read_sav("mm.sav")

prepped <- prep_mics_sib_histories(mm, survey = "IQ2018")

prepped$ego.dat   # one row per respondent
prepped$sib.dat   # one row per reported sibling
prepped$summ      # a one-row summary

survey should have a code that identifies the survey – e.g., ZW2014. DHS surveys include this code in the datafiles, but MICS surveys do not, so you have to supply it here.

For MICS4 or MICS5 data, pass the matching varmap:

prep_mics_sib_histories(mm, survey = "ZW2014", varmap = sibhist_varmap_mics5)

Some countries omit the respondent’s date of birth from mm.sav. When that happens, supply the women’s file so respondent age can be recovered:

prep_mics_sib_histories(mm, survey = "MDG2018", wm.df = read_sav("wm.sav"))

Special features of MICS files

MICS files differ from DHS files in several ways; prep_mics_sib_histories() handles all of the following.

Weights are already normalized. The DHS publishes women’s weights multiplied by 1,000,000; MICS wmweight column, on the other hand, averages 1. The MICS prep therefore defaults to weight.scale = 1. Passing DHS-style scaling here would divide every weight by a million, and nothing downstream would complain.

Survival status is coded differently. MICS codes MM16 as 1 yes / 2 no / 8 don’t know, while this package follows the DHS convention of 1 alive / 0 dead. The prep file recodes this.

Don’t-know values are codes, not blanks. MICS uses 98 and 99 on the numeric items (MM17 age, MM18 years since death, MM19 age at death). Left as-is, a sibling with sib.death.age = 98 gets a date of birth 98 years before her death. This is masked whenever MICS supplies its own imputed CMC dates, so it only affects surveys that ship no imputed CMC dates. The prep function will set these to NA.

MM16 collides with the DHS. In MICS6, the mm16 variable is the survey question that asks “Is (name) still alive?”; in DHS phase 7 and later mm16 is the survey question that asks “died of violence or an accident”. To avoid errors resulting from confusing these two, the prep function refuses to run a varmap that maps mm16 to sib.died.accident.

Several columns must be constructed. MICS has no single respondent id, so caseid is built from cluster, household and line number. doi comes from WDOI where present and is otherwise built from the interview year and month; it must end up a century month code, since all the date derivations are integer arithmetic in months. Respondent age is derived from WDOI and WDOB, psu falls back to the cluster (only 4 of the 13 usable surveys carry a psu column), and sex is set to 'f', since MICS interviews only women.

Names are mixed case. Questionnaire items and link keys are uppercase (MM15, HH1, WDOI) while derived and design variables are lowercase (wmweight, psu, welevel). The varmaps are lowercase, so lowercase = TRUE is used to normalize the input.

Sibling dates may or may not be supplied. MICS6 usually includes MM17C and MM18C (imputed CMC birth and death dates), and MICS4/5 includes MM7C and MM8C, but some countries include neither. The package uses them when present and approximates them from reported ages and years-since-death otherwise.

Validation against published estimates

We evaluated code in the package by comparing its estimates to published tables from three MICS6 surveys and one MICS5 survey.

First, we examing quantities that are essentially sums over survey responses. The following table shows ratios of the value produced by the package to the value published in the MICS report:

Iraq 2018 Madagascar 2018 Zimbabwe 2014 Zimbabwe 2019
Round MICS6 MICS6 MICS5 MICS6
Female exposure 0.9999 1.0003 0.9995 0.9966
Male exposure 0.9993 1.0003 0.9994 0.9990
Female all-cause deaths 1.0007 0.9994 1.0037 0.9867
Male all-cause deaths 0.9996 1.0003 1.0015 1.0023
Pregnancy-related deaths 1.0068 0.9967 1.0002 0.8962

The pregnancy-related row uses the postpartum window each round’s own published tables use: preg.window = "42days" for the three MICS6 surveys and the two-month default for Zimbabwe 2014, since MICS5 asks no day count and its reports use the wider definition. The next section explains why.

The values are generally very close, with the exception of the count of pregnancy-related deaths in the Zimbabwe 2019 survey, which is discussed below.

Next, we examined the extent to which estimated mortality rates agree between the package and the MICS reports. These quantities are more complex; they are ratios, some involve standarizing by the respondents’ age distribution, and some involve life table calculations. Note that these rates all come from the aggregate visibility estimator; the individual visibility estimator has not been used in any MICS reports.

This table shows the estimates produced by the package, along with estimates published in MICS reports in parentheses:

Iraq 2018 Madagascar 2018 Zimbabwe 2014 Zimbabwe 2019
All-cause rate, womena^a 1.25 (1.25) 3.08 (3.1) 9.98 (9.84) 6.27 (6.28)
All-cause rate, mena^a 2.39 (2.39) 4.03 (4.0) 9.90 (9.79) 6.16 (6.09)
Pregnancy-related ratea^a 0.133 (0.13) 0.650 (0.65) 0.862 (0.86) 0.530 (0.59)
35q15_{35}q_{15}, womenb^b 49.5 (49) 111.9 (112) 345.0 (344) 222.7 (224)
35q15_{35}q_{15}, menb^b 85.8 (86) 148.8 (149) 356.7 (357) 218.5 (219)

Here, estimates produced by the package match estimates in the MICS reports quite closely.

What the official tabulation syntax says

UNICEF distributes the SPSS syntax used to produce the MICS6 report tables. One file, MICS6 - 06 - TM.9.1&TM.9.2&TM.9.3&DQ.7.1&DQ7.2.sps, produces the whole mortality group. Transcribing it literally into R – see data-raw/mics-validation/spss-syntax-replica.R – settles several questions that the reports themselves leave open, and it reproduces Iraq 2018 and Madagascar 2018 to the person-year:

Iraq 2018 Madagascar 2018
Female exposure 471,294 (471,294) 202,959 (202,959)
Male exposure 485,398 (485,398) 208,274 (208,274)
Female all-cause deaths 574.4 (574) 616.6 (617)
Pregnancy-related deaths 64.4 (64) 136.6 (137)
General fertility rate 128.2 (128) —
Maternal mortality ratio 104.0 (104) —

The published “maternal deaths” column is a 42-day pregnancy-related count

The syntax flags a death with

if (MM15 = 2 & (MM22 = 1 or MM23 = 1 or (MM24 = 1 and MM25 < 42))) md = 1.

MM26 (violence) and MM27 (accident) are never read anywhere in the file, even though the reports carry a footnote saying deaths from those causes are excluded. So what is printed under “Maternal Deaths” is a pregnancy-related count restricted to a 42-day postpartum window – which is the WHO definition of a pregnancy-related death, and is neither of the two things this package used to compute. On Iraq 2018 the three candidate definitions give:

Definition Deaths Ratio to published 64
MM22 \| MM23 \| MM24 – two months, any cause 67.7 1.057
MM22 \| MM23 \| (MM24 & MM25 < 42) – 42 days, any cause 64.4 1.007
… additionally excluding MM26/MM27 – our maternal column 59.0 0.922

add_maternal_deaths(preg.window = "42days") selects the middle row, and is what you want when comparing against a published MICS table. The default stays "2months", which is the wider DHS-comparable reading. Note that the 42-day cut is also what the package has always applied on the DHS side, through the mm12 band 100–141.

Other conventions the syntax fixes

  • The seven-year window is [wdoi - 84, wdoi - 1]: the interview month is excluded. cell_config(time.periods = '7yr_beforeinterview') already does this.
  • Age standardisation uses the weighted age distribution of women with a completed interview (WM17 = 1), which is what get_ego_age_distn() computes.
  • A decedent’s exposure ends the month before death (MM18C - 1), and the death is assigned to the age group holding at that month rather than to the age at death.
  • Siblings whose survival status is unknown are kept, contributing full exposure. This package drops them instead, which is why our exposure totals sit within about 0.1% of the published ones rather than exactly on them — Iraq has 107 such siblings, Zimbabwe 2019 has 42, Madagascar only 9.
  • 35q15_{35}q_{15} is computed with 1 + 2.4*nmx in the denominator, i.e. nax=2.6n_ax = 2.6, although the same file’s header documents nax=2.5n_ax = 2.5. The difference is at most 0.2 per 1,000 and cannot be resolved against published figures, which are rounded to integers.

Zimbabwe 2019

Running the official syntax on Zimbabwe 2019’s own public microdata reproduces its male columns and fails on its female ones:

Ours Published Ratio
Male exposure 110,072 110,089 0.9998
Male all-cause deaths 669.5 668 1.002
Male all-cause rate 6.087 6.09 0.9995
Female exposure 108,644 108,985 0.9969
Female all-cause deaths 665.7 674 0.988
Pregnancy-related deaths 60.9 68 0.896

Both sexes go through identical code, differing only in which value of MM15 they select on, so a data-handling difference that hits one and not the other is not something the calculation can produce. No variation on the window, the age restriction, the weighting, or the treatment of the 17 sex-missing rows brings the female figures up to the published ones.

The report also contradicts itself. Its sampling-error appendix gives a maternal mortality ratio (indicator TM.21) of 413.64, against 462 in TM.9.3. Those two figures come from different implementations – the appendix notes that maternal mortality ratio errors “can be calculated only through the separate CS Pro application” – and it is the appendix that we reproduce: the official syntax on the public microdata gives 409.9, within 1% of 413.64 and 11% below the headline. The fertility side of the same table reproduces exactly (our GFR 128.4 against a published 128), so the discrepancy is confined to the female sibling records.

Zimbabwe 2014 reproduces essentially exactly – its pregnancy-related death count comes out at 1.0002 of the published figure – so this is specific to the 2019 survey’s published tables rather than to the country. Treat Zimbabwe 2019’s published female mortality figures as unreliable.

Running every survey through the prep

All 13 MICS surveys with a sibling roster have been run through the prep. Every one completes, produces no NA estimates, and gives a plausible pregnancy-related rate (0.07 to 1.46 per 1,000 woman-years). Two turned up country-specific data quirks worth knowing about:

  • São Tomé and Príncipe 2014 has one respondent with no sampling weight, and names its weight column WMWEIGHT rather than wmweight. That single weightless respondent used to make sum(wwgt) NA inside get_ego_age_distn(), which propagated through the denominator and turned every group proportion NA – silently NA-ing out every age-standardised rate for the survey. Such respondents are now dropped, with a warning.
  • Bhutan 2010 contains two siblings whose reported years-since-death and age at death are jointly inconsistent – one died 58 years ago at age 58, implying a birth 116 years before the interview. The prep function warns rather than silently carrying it.

Rows that cannot contribute to a weighted estimate – no usable date of birth, or no sampling weight – are dropped, and counted in summ$miss.dob and summ$miss.wgt.

What will not necessarily agree with reports, by design

  • asdr.ind. This estimator is not used in MICS reports.
  • Siblings of unknown survival status. The package drops them; the official syntax keeps them at full exposure. This is the main reason exposure totals land within about 0.1% of published ones rather than exactly on them.
  • Confidence intervals. MICS uses jackknife replication with ±2⋅se\pm 2 \cdot se; this package uses a bootstrap with percentile intervals.
  • The maternal mortality ratio itself. MMR is the maternal mortality rate divided by a general fertility rate computed from the women’s birth history – a different module this package does not read. (The replica script does compute it, for validation purposes only.)

Maternal versus pregnancy-related

MICS6 and MICS7 ask whether the death was due to violence (MM26) or an accident (MM27), so both estimands are computable. MICS4 and MICS5 do not, so they support pregnancy-related mortality only – the same limitation as DHS phases 2–6.

Because MICS6 also records the number of days after the end of pregnancy (MM25), the older two-month pregnancy-related series can be reconstructed from MICS6 microdata. That is what makes MICS6 comparable with DHS surveys and with earlier MICS rounds.

There are really three quantities in play, and it is worth being explicit about which one is wanted:

Postpartum window Excludes violence/accident? How to get it
Pregnancy-related, DHS-comparable two months no preg.window = "2months" (default)
Pregnancy-related, WHO / published MICS 42 days no preg.window = "42days"
Maternal 42 days yes sib.maternal.death.date

The middle row is what MICS6 and MICS7 reports print, however they are labelled.

MICS4 and MICS5 never ask MM25, so only the first row is available for them — and it is also the right one, since the syntax’s own header notes that in earlier rounds “maternal deaths were defined as deaths of women during pregnancy or childbirth or within two months after the termination of a pregnancy or childbirth, inclusive of all causes”. Asking for preg.window = "42days" on MICS4/5 data is an error rather than a silent no-op.

Three questionnaire skip patterns must be respected when classifying deaths:

  • MM23 = 1 (died during childbirth) skips MM26 and MM27 entirely, so those are NA by design. A childbirth death is unconditionally maternal and must not be excluded for missing cause information.
  • MM21 routes sisters who died before age 12 past MM22–MM25, so those items are also NA by design. An explicit age guard is needed, or every under-12 female death is counted as maternal.
  • MM16 = DK jumps to the next sibling with no age or date information at all.
